why: A natural is a known mixture of mostly common materials, so it can be built from its GC composition and scored as a sub-mixture instead of being dropped. This matters for coverage: across the 22 published patent formulas, naturals are 6316 g of the 13362 g the library could not resolve, and bergamot alone is 2084 g of it.
caveat: A composition is a chemotype, not a substance. The four lavenders below share a name and differ enough to smell like different materials, and the model ranks them accordingly. Any formula that just says 'lavender oil' is therefore underspecified, and picking a chemotype for it is an assumption the prediction inherits.
unbuildable: Treemoss, patchouli, vetiver and the resinoids stay out of reach: their character sits in atranol-type phenolics, patchoulol and sesquiterpene alcohols that the library does not hold, so building them from the fraction that is available would misrepresent them more than dropping them does.

lavender oil, L. angustifolia commercial.source: GC-MS of commercial market samples; linalyl acetate 37.8, linalool 33.1, eucalyptol 4.9, camphor 4.1. Minor terpenes added from the same literature range.
lavender oil, L. angustifolia commercial.note: The default for an unqualified 'lavender oil' in a perfumery formula.
lavender oil, L. angustifolia commercial.omitted: terpinen-4-ol (~2%) and lavandulyl acetate are not in the library

lavender oil, L. angustifolia Spanish va.source: linalool 38.0, borneol 19.7, camphor 8.1, cineole ~3, linalyl acetate ~1.1

lavender oil, South African.note: Barely a lavender by odour, and the model places it with Camphor rather than with the linalyl esters.
